en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Rattandhakāravagga 13.
The Training Rule on Conversing Outdoors At that time the Buddha,
the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a relative of the nun Bhaddā Kāpilānī’s pupil had come from a village to Sāvatthī on some business.
Then that nun, thinking,
“The Blessed One has prohibited standing or conversing with a man alone in a concealed place,” nevertheless stood and conversed with that very man alone in the open air.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... they were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can a bhikkhunī stand and converse alone with a man in the open air? ... [The Buddha asked:
"Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī stands and converses alone with a man in the open air?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can this be, monks? How can a bhikkhunī stand or converse alone with a man in the open air?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [as before] … And thus,
monks, should the nuns recite this training rule:
‘If any bhikkhunī should stand or converse alone with a man in an open space, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whichever" means whichever such... "nun" means...
[as before]... nun.
...pe... this is the nun intended in this context.
"In the open air" means it is uncovered by a wall, or a door-panel, or a palm-leaf screen, or a cloth fence, or a tree, or a pillar, or a granary; that is, it is not covered by anything whatsoever.
"A person" means a human being, not a *yakkha*, not a *peta*, and not an animal; one who is wise and capable of standing and conversing.
"Together with" (*saddhiṃ*)...
On one side.
"One with one" means it is both a man and a bhikkhunī.
"Should stand still" means:
if she stands within arm's reach of a man, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
"Should converse" means: [if she converses].
If she stands or converses within arm’s reach of a man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she stands or converses after having left arm’s reach, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she stands or converses with a yakkha, a peta, a paṇḍaka, or one who is an animal in human form, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if there is some other person who understands as a companion,
or if one is indifferent toward the goal.
If she stands together with or converses with someone else while being distracted—
provided she is insane or it is her first offense.
The third training rule is concluded.
